name: Driftmend Hooded Rain Cloak — Patchwork Cut
description: A floor-length hooded cloak assembled from irregular panels of secondhand waterproof synthetics — dusty olive, faded burgundy, and industrial grey — each panel seam-sealed with thermal bonding tape. The oversized hood fits over basic horn and ear geneware without modification. Worn loose and layered, it signals resourceful self-sufficiency rather than poverty.
functionality: Full-length rain and wind protection with generous hood clearance for minor geneware; tail-slit option available at street tailors.
what_it_says: Someone who builds their own solutions and doesn't apologize for the seams showing.
story_hooks: One panel is cut from a Stratum Logistics uniform — the wearer might have worked there once, or might have taken it off someone who did.
The cloak is three sizes too large for the person wearing it and still fits perfectly — made for someone else, passed down or taken.

physical_description.visual_profile: A dramatic floor-length silhouette that reads as both protective and deliberately assembled. The cloak drapes heavily from broad shoulders, creating a shadowy, layered appearance that obscures the wearer's frame entirely. The oversized hood dominates the profile—deep and cave-like, designed to accommodate cranial augmentations without pressure or distortion. The irregular patchwork of mismatched panel colors creates visual movement despite the garment's stillness.
physical_description.fit: Deliberately oversized and unstructured, designed to layer over street gear without binding. The hood sits loose enough for horn or ear geneware but snug enough to stay secure in wind or crowd movement. No tailoring to specific body proportions—intentionally universal fit. Excess fabric pools slightly at the ankles, meant to be worn dragging or folded.
physical_description.primary_material: Recycled and salvaged waterproof synthetics—likely reclaimed from medical textiles, cargo wraps, and industrial protective gear. Panels are heat-sealed together using thermal bonding tape (visible as raised black seams) rather than traditional stitching.
physical_description.texture: Each panel has distinct surface variation: some smooth and slightly glossy from factory weatherproofing, others dulled and micro-creased from years of use. The thermal bonding seams create rigid linear ridges. Overall tactile impression is industrial and utilitarian—nothing soft or plush.
physical_description.color_scheme: A muted trinity of post-industrial tones: dusty olive (dominant, appears khaki-greyed from age), faded burgundy (wine-darkened, almost mauve in shadow), and industrial grey (cool, slightly blue-shifted). No bright accents—all colors appear sun-faded or chemically aged. Panels are arranged asymmetrically with no apparent logic, enhancing the 'salvaged' quality.
physical_description.closures: None visible. The cloak is worn open, draping freely. The hood likely has interior friction-fit adjustment tabs or drawcords (not prominent) to secure fit around augmented heads without needing visible fasteners.
distinctive_features: Irregular panel geometry—no two seams are parallel, creating dynamic visual rhythm
Visible thermal bonding tape seams in matte black, creating industrial grid overlays
Hood designed with extra depth and width at crown, sloping back slightly to accommodate cranial hardware
Asymmetrical hem, dragging longer on one side (intentional design or evolved wear)
Possibly faded manufacturer tags or serial numbers still visible on interior panels (Tier 5 authenticity marker)
Thermal-sealed repair patches on lower panels—evidence of field mending
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 / Sub-grade street gear. The garment's value is in its functionality and the resourcefulness of its assembly, not material luxury. However, the intentional design sophistication elevates it above mere survival wear—it's *styled* poverty, not desperation.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by street operators, independent couriers, sub-grade augmentation clinicians, and urban nomads who move between ungoverned zones. Signals practical self-sufficiency, rejection of corpo-standardization, and likely involvement in informal/grey-market economy. The accommodation for geneware suggests the wearer is modded and outside formal corpo registry. Also worn by artists and provocateurs who aestheticize DIY culture.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn but maintained. Not pristine—the garment is meant to look weathered and assembled. However, the thermal seams are intact and the hood's function is uncompromised. Shows age and street exposure (dust stains, minor discoloration) but no major rips or deterioration. The patchwork nature means wear is camouflaged by the design itself.
